title: P-645 Melatonin supplementation during controlled ovarian stimulation for women undergoing assisted reproductive technology: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract:
Is there any available evidence on the effect of melatonin supplementation during controlled ovarian stimulation (COS) on assisted reproductive technology (ART) outcomes?

Melatonin supplementation improve oocyte maturation rate, and embryo quality, and clinical pregnancy rates in assisted reproduction.

Melatonin, a hormone synthesized mainly by the pineal gland and secreted during the night, plays a key role in regulating biological rhythms, such as inducing sleep. It also possesses antioxidant properties, potential anticarcinogenic effects, and a protective role against neurodegenerative diseases. Owing to its well-established antioxidant properties, melatonin supplementation has been posited as a valuable adjunct to in vitro fertilisation (IVF) protocols, given that oxidative stress is known to compromise treatment success. Furthermore, melatonin exerts a critical regulatory function within the antral follicle, directing steroidogenesis and modulating the mRNA expression of luteinising hormone (LH) and maturation-inducing hormone.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) was performed in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook and PRISMA guidelines. The search included studies from inception to August 2024. All eligible RCTs comparing melatonin supplementation versus no melatonin in infertile patients undergoing COS for ART were included.

For this, the PICO framework was applied: Population: patients undergoing ART; Intervention: melatonin use; Comparison: no melatonin use; Outcomes (Primary): live births and clinical pregnancy; (Secondary): number of retrieved oocytes and embryo quality. Bias Risk was assessed using RoB 2.0. Continuous outcomes were reported as mean differences (MDs) or standardised mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals. A fixed-effect or random-effects model was employed as appropriate, and between-study heterogeneity was evaluated using the I² statistic.

A total of 562 references were initially identified, of which only 26 underwent full-text assessment after excluding those not meeting the inclusion criteria. From these 26 references, pilot studies, non-randomised trials, those employing different methodologies, or those involving melatonin use in the culture medium were excluded, leaving a total of 14 references. Among these 14 references, in two studies both treatment groups received melatonin. Therefore, this meta-analysis included 12 studies with a total of 833 participants in the melatonin group and 753 in the control group. Melatonin supplementation significantly increased clinical pregnancy rates (0.08, 95% CI: 0.04 to 0.12; p < 0.0001), and improved the number of mature oocytes (1.47, 95% CI: 0.30 to 2.65; p = 0.01) and embryo quality (0.58, 95% CI: 0.24 to 0.92; p = 0.0008). No statistically significant differences were found in live birth rates or total oocyte retrieval, and melatonin did not increase the risk of miscarriage.

Although multiple studies were analysed, many had relatively small sample sizes and varying methodological quality, limiting the strength of the conclusions.

These findings suggest that melatonin supplementation may enhance certain IVF outcomes, such as clinical pregnancy rates and embryo quality. Incorporating melatonin into current ART protocols could improve patient counselling, refine clinical strategies, and potentially inform future research directions aiming to optimise fertility treatments.
